I want to welcome everybody to today's DAU event.
This is CADE for the contracting community.
My name is Emmett Simmons.
I'm the producer for today's event.
A couple of quick items, your microphones will be muted throughout the session.
This session is being recorded and will be posted
to dau.edu/dau-webcast which is listed at the bottom.

>> Great, thank you, Emmett.
I appreciate it very much, and again thank you for joining us today.
We have looks like a little over 70, almost 80 people on today
for the CADE's CADE training team.

This is the sixth webcast.

We now call them webcasts on the CADE -- from the CADE training team, and we're always happy
to have them come back and present.
Oh, just as a note, we'll be working a future event, so keep your eye out on the webpage
for DAU for webcasts, and we will be presenting future topics.
We just completed a topic on CADE for program managers.
We went over it extremely well, and we had many people not only instructors, but professors
and also practitioners from the various program offices attend that session,
so I think it was a very successful time as the CADE team will articulate, they --
we at DAU are only part of the training programs that they have, and so they will articulate
that throughout or within the briefings today, but we're happy to join them
as since we have worked so closely over the years on everything from FlexFiles
and other topics that they have taught, so without further ado,
I'm going to turn it over to the CADE team.
Welcome, gentlemen, and it's good to see you, and I'll turn it over to you.
Over.
>> Great, thank you, everybody.
So I'll be kicking it off today.
My name is Jack Titus.
I'm a member of the CADE training team, as well as the defense and cost and resource center.
You'll be hearing also in the DSR.
You'll be hearing that a couple of times today, but wanted to get us kicked off
on so just can someone give me a quick thumbs up,
make sure you're seeing our slide one on the screen currently.
>> Yes, Jack.
We're seeing it just fine.
>> Awesome.
Great. Thank you, so just a quick slide one.
Wanted to give you a couple of links, definitely some of the key ones we'll be talking about
and those that you can use for a variety
of different other training options, so the first one being CADE.
That's going to be the magic link today, all of our resources,
a lot of information can be found on that website.
Next, and then about a couple seconds, we're using Poll Everywhere during today's training,
just to kind of keep you interactive, understand our audience,
the kind of questions you may have, and the lastly, we'll go into a little bit it
at the end, but our bridge learning management system.
If you're interested in today's course, and you want to learn more about CSDR,
we do offer a variety of different courses in our bridge LMS
so you can access either an account through that link,
or you can send a request via the CADE website as well.
And with that, I hope everyone in the room today we are doing a CADE
for the contracting community, so to start, I'm actually going to open up one of those poll EVs
that I mentioned, so again, hopefully you are seeing my screen.
I'm moving over to the first poll that we'll have today.
So again, this poll will be software just to kind of keep it interactive with you all,
just to see who we have on line and we'll kind of gauge any kind
of questions you may have throughout the presentation.
So the first one, if you're if you're not on screenshare.
we're using the link pollev.com/ttraining456.
There's a up there just saying what is your role?
So we kind of say who all's on the phone today, seeing some answers
in the chat and that's great too.
The options are A) Contracting Officer, B) contracting specialist, C) cost price analyst
and then D) other so seeing a couple -- a lot of Cs and Ds are currently on the poll itself.
A couple of a lot of As and Bs in the chat,
so those we have a pretty widespread group people on the line and that's great.
We'll definitely touch areas of interest for all parties today.
Just kind of wanted to gauge exactly who all was on the line today so awesome,
and definitely appreciate the feedback there.
Okay. With that, I'm actually going to go to the next poll.
Again, just kind of branching out in terms of understanding who all we have reaching
that CADE network, so kind of more of an open question,
but what organization are you coming from?
It'll create a word chart or a word cloud on the screen, so great, seeing some DCAA,
DC and some whether you're from the program office, seeming some AFLCMC.
It's great.
I'm seeing a lot of different options now.
That's good to see we're wide span of folks on the line today.
Awesome. I'm seeing some DLA in the chat as well, some Joint Staff, SSP.
That's great.
Awesome, and the last poll to get everyone warmed up, and then definitely so we can hit any
and all questions either during the lesson or in we can also [inaudible] but wanted
to understand exactly what all you are hoping to gain from today's training,
so maybe you are interested in CADE for Contracting Officers because you want
to learn more about CADE, the CSDRs, how it may relate to what you all do for your day job.
We're just trying to understand exactly maybe some of those nuances so we can answer them,
and definitely [inaudible] during our lesson today, so great,
seeing some what CADE has to offer.
I would say plenty, so we'll definitely go into that today, and tools of the toolbox,
always good to improve things that you're already working on so that's great.
Data, that we definitely have a lot of that in our cases, so in the form of CSDRs.
That's a great point there as well.
Again, in the chat, just seeing a lot of different CSDR plus CADE information.
We can definitely provide that today.
Policy, we'll definitely hit on all this.
That's great stuff, so when we get these kind of topics in our presentations,
we definitely will channel back these kind of points of emphasis,
just so everyone understands how that kind of relates
to those different fields we talked about today.
Awesome. So with that, I'm going to bounce back to my presentation, and I think from there,
I'll turn it over to my colleague, Mr. Torri Preston.
>> Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, again, my name is Torri Preston.
I'm the CADE training and outreach lead.
Again, I always appreciate the opportunity for us to engage with DAU
and utilize their platform to engage.
Again, you know, this quick slide is just a overview of some of the presenters that we have,
and then Jack, move on to the objectives slide please.
>> Yup, on slide seven.
>> All right, great.
So again, kind of how we mentioned, right?
-- particularly for today's training, we want to figure out a way to kind of help convey how,
you know, the cases that can be beneficial for the contracting community, so again, you know,
we kind of bucket it down into three kind of primary buckets in terms of justifying fair
and reasonable price, you know, efficiency in the proposal analysis, as well as how to gain
that negotiation power, and again, you know, the bumper sticker on here is the overall intent is
for us to kind of figure out the best way to allow, you know, the best, you know,
estimates on the overall contract.
So on slide eight, you know, the contracting and cost partnership, again,
this is something that's been around for a while.
You know, we've always kind of tried to leverage the amount of, you know,
joint efforts for to kind of force the contracting and cost community partnership.
I know some of you may have had opportunity to attend the 2016 joint contracting
and cost conference, and again, you know,
DAU has also facilitated several different corollaries between, you know, how we improve,
you know, our training and certification criteria,
not only at DAU but in NPS and AFIT as well.
You know, some of you have probably come across you know, the community body of knowledge
with regards to revisions to the GAO cost estimating guide.
Those who have attended, ICEAA conferences in the past,
as well as some of the government contract management symposiums.
You know, we've always tried our best to look for different avenues to kind
of continue to foster that relationship.
For those who haven't had the opportunity or aren't familiar with the contract database,
again, this tool has provided, you know, a wide myriad of, you know, information to kind
of help facilitate some of the information that you,
from across the contracting community perspective, can find very beneficial.
So you know, we try to continue to leverage that relationship and always look for opportunities
to grow and expand, you know, whether it's all of the word charts on the right hand side,
you know, all the different acronyms that we go about but, you know,
us understanding who we are, and us understanding where those corollaries are,
I think, go a long way, within terms of how we can continue to foster this relationship,
so we'll move on to slide nine, so this is actually going to be sent out in an attachment
as well where you can download it and kind of keeping it in your hip pocket, but essentially,
you know, we tried to create a handy reference for, you know, cost reporting
and contract data requirements list or our C rules, just so you can kind of determine,
you know, what different levels
and what different reports are required at those levels, right?
So you know, this document will try to reference throughout the training, but again,
it's something that we'll make sure that you have access to just as a handy guide
to help kind of facilitate some of these conversations, you know, with you,
as well as some other people in your program.
Okay, so we'll make our way to slide -- to the next slide.
So types of CSDRs, and FlexFiles so you know, before we get started, we just kind of want
to give, you know, the CSDR background, and, you know, just some of the nuances with regards
to what reports actually make up, you know, the, the CSDR.
So again, you know, CSDRs are, you know, costing software data reports, you know?
They're comprised of, you know, a few different types of reports where, you know,
you have your contractor cost data reports, or your CCDRs, you know,
on the on the right hand side in light blue,
and then you have your software resource data reports, and then your other technical reports,
you know, on the left hand side, in dark blue, so again, while CSDRs, they're always going
to be a good idea, you know, to consider on your contracts, there are certain things
that make it mandatory, so first and foremost, you know, with the 2017 NDA, you know,
CSDRs are generally required for all programs with the lifecycle costs, you know,
that's greater than that $100 million threshold, and with that exceed that $50 million threshold,
so as we kind of orient ourselves on this chart, we'll start with the CSDR plan, or the 2794,
so the CSDR plan is not a type of CSDR but it's essentially, kind of the rules of the road
that lay out the, you know, the work breakdown structure and kind of help ensure
that the reporting requirements in the structure are kind of properly defined,
not only for costs, but for software and the technical reporting requirements given
to the contract, as well as the contractor.
So there are three types of plans.
You have your program plan that outlines the scope
of the program, you know, at a specific phase.
You have that contract plan that outlines the reporting requirements for the prime contractor,
and then you have a subcontract plan that kind of outlines the reporting requirements
that are actually flowed down to the subcontractors from the prime.
So on our little wheel here, moving kind of clockwise, we'll talk about some of the CCDRs.
So you know, first and foremost the cost and hour report or the FlexFile,
I know a lot of you may have seen this name in orders come up on some of your contracts,
but essentially, it's the primary mechanism for reporting actual costs and hours
in accordance to, you know, your CLIN, the company's rate structure as well
as a product oriented work breakdown structure.
So the unique thing about the FlexFile, you know, it's time phased by month.
It provides insight at what we call the account level,
so where the contractor actually incurs the cost to their system, you know, ultimately,
this level will kind of get determined by the contractor,
but it's going to most likely take the shape of either a control account, a charge number,
a work package or something along those lines.
So moving continuing clockwise, you know, the quantity report, because the FlexFile is kind
of primarily a financial report, it did make it necessary to create a separate report that kind
of captures the relevant quantity information, you know,
with those kind of synchronized definitions and references
between the different DDs and the data model.
So essentially the quantity report kind of ties the necessary quantity information
to the FlexFile, and again, these quantities are, you know, are tagged by WBS, order lot,
and end items, we kind of makes it possible to make those discrete ties.
Okay, continuing clockwise, we'll go down to the contract business data report or the 1921-3.
So again, this is a system for kind of collecting that direct and indirect costs
in our employee data at the business level, so you know, this is a broken out in terms
of the contractor's own proposed categories.
You know, the report kind of also includes some of that summary level capacity labor
and sales data, but essentially the 1921-3 kind of assists with the development of some
of those good old independent government cost assessments,
as well as some of the relevant cost in price analysis,
as well as hopefully aiding you all in, you know, some of those contract negotiations,
so it kind of gives the basis for an assessment of, you know, a contractor's overhead,
cost status during, you know, the progression of the contract, and it kind of gives context to,
you know, the overall posture, rather than just express that, you know, some specific
or nonspecific rate of some base.
So continuing on, we'll talk through some of the technical report.
So again, the maintenance and repair report, you know, these are used by contractors
to submit maintenance event data, and again, this is related to, you know,
each of the maintenance events, you know, such as a specific system being prepared,
the location where it took place, as well as the reason for failure and, you know,
other kind of maintenance-related information as well in that M&R report.
All right, and then we'll jump to the software resource data report.
So last, we'll go to technical data first.
So the technical data report, you know, it actually provides a mechanism for us to kind
of capture, you know, some of that tech data on contracts.
It does kind of normalize a common kind of technical data vocabulary,
and definitely defines that core set of the parameters that we need, you know?
It also leverages, like other technical data on the contract.
You know, it essentially, you know, allows us to kind of review
and evaluate a program's technical baseline, and also kind of describe the technical parameters
that are required to help develop, you know, the program lifecycle cost estimate,
and other kind of programmatic and technical information, kind of in support of, you know,
that trade-off analysis, and some of those cost analysis activities.
And, finally, we'll talk through some of the SSDR, so again, you know, the SSDR,
it actually kind of provides insight on the size, schedule and effort on, you know,
some of the software development programs.
Software reports, you know, they're required on any of the contracts where, you know,
the software development effort exceeds the $20 million threshold.
And, you know, it also provides data that can be like --
because certain data, it can kind of help us.
We can collect without CSDRs, but then others, you know, the software portion of the effort,
if it doesn't necessarily reach that threshold, it's not going to be --
so a SRDR is essentially never going to be collected without,
you know, the corresponding CCDR.
So again, the software report, you know, gives us insight into the size, the schedule
and the effort of that software development project but again,
it's never going to be collected without that corresponding CCDR.
All right.
So moving ahead, so some of the types of CSDRs when we talk legacy, it's basically essentially,
you know, the legacy reports, you know, they're essentially these C rules kind
of take the place of, you know, any event that you're still reporting legacy, you know,
they would take the place of that FlexFile and quantity report we just described.
So again, very, very similar contract work breakdown structure,
it kind of lists the contract data requirement report elements, and again,
this defines the technical, the work and the cost content, and again, you know,
the purpose behind, you know, the CWS dictionary is to kind
of document the contractor's plan approach, as well as kind of, you know,
how they're going to perform the actual contract scope of work.
The Cost Data Summary Report, or the DD 1921, again, this is kind of that summary cost data
for all the elements on the approved contract CSDR.
It does contain the cost, both to-date and at completion, and again, this is further broken
out by a non-recurring and recurring categories.
You know, this report, it also contains some of the quantities, you know,
number of units to-date, at completion, for some of the hardware elements, and again, you know,
the, the 1921 form also kind of includes some of those summary elements, you know,
broken out discreetly, you know, at the end of the report.
So again, very valuable resource here with regards to the Cost Data Summary Report.
The functional cost and hour report or the 1921-1, it kind of further breaks out, you know,
the hours into the, you know, functional labor categories, you know, specifically engineering,
manufacturing, quality control and tooling, and again, one of the kind of big takeaways
for the 1921-1, it kind of enables three different types of analysis, whether that's the,
you know, labor versus material, hours versus dollars and, you know,
the type of work being done with regards to, you know, engineering, manufacturing,
etc. The sustainment report, or the 1921-5 is essentially broken out the same way
as the 1921-1, except the functional categories are kind
of aligned towards more sustainment type activities.
You know, those functional categories are, you know, your engineering, program management,
touch maintenance, support maintenance, and things of that nature.
So in a given effort, you know, you either have a 1921-1 or a 1921-5, but not both.
All right, and then, so, for our progress curve report or our 1921-2, again, you know,
the lot or unit reporting, you know, of the direct recurring costs to-date, you know,
for specific hardware elements, for this one,
the kind of big key takeaway is it helps facilitate that learning curve analysis.
So again, this data is broken out discreetly by completed units or lots, and again,
it does help facilitate, you know, that learning curve analysis.
All right, so, again, we've kind of covered, you know, the majority of the legacy reports.
We want to keep things.
We want to try to note is that, obviously, what's in the legacy reports is also captured
in the FlexFile, but next, we'll move on to Slide 12,
and just kind of talk quickly about, you know, why should you comply?
So outside of it being because it's the law,
there's a myriad of actually policy that's associated with, you know,
why a person should comply, right?
So I know a lot of you are familiar with the, you know,
the weapon system acquisition format back in 2009, but it essentially, you know, gave CADE,
you know, the responsibility of performing these cost estimates and analysis
for acquisition programs but, you know, starting on the far left, you know, we mentioned early
on in the 2017 NDAA, you know, inserted a new paragraph
that essentially requires cost data collection for acquisition programs
over that $100 million threshold, right?
So again, Mike knows, you know, I'm a Marine by trade, and obviously,
Marines kind of love colors, right?
So just to kind of orient you on the sections of this chart,
everything that's in yellow essentially describes the documents that mandate reporting.
The items that are in green kind of highlight what you need to report, thresholds,
the details, how to fill out forms, things of that nature.
The items in orange kind of show how you need to report, right?
So the details on the schedule, the WS and kind of what's allocated in the [inaudible],
and then the things in blue are the details of what you're actually reporting.
So if we circle back to the items that are in yellow, obviously, the DFARS establishes
that CSDR policy and, again, you know, three primary clauses we should be concerned
with in the contract is that, you know, obviously, first, you know,
all costs must reflect, you know,
the actual transactional costs to the maximum extent possible.
The second thing is that, you know, the contractors must discuss their approach
to execute the CSDR reporting, and then the last thing is that a, you know,
program ratings review, formerly known as a post award conference, must take place to kind
of discuss the intent of reporting, and then this kind of gives the opportunity
for contractors to express their concerns.
The 5000.02, again, we mentioned that that kind of will state the thresholds that are outlined,
you know, for reporting and, you know, its interpretation of what's
in the contract, you know, necessary.
It also outlines the request for waivers.
Obviously, you know, waivers can kind of only take place, you know, if, you know, a, you know,
a firm fixed-price contract was awarded, you know, for, you know,
procurement of a commercial item that was, you know,
competitively awarded, so we want to keep that in mind.
Waivers occur, not frequently, but again, you know, there is a process outlined in terms
of how you execute those waivers in the 5000.02.
The 5000.73 is kind of going to define the CSDR reporting thresholds, and as we mentioned,
the 5000.04 is going to outline the process for CSDR planning and execution,
which we'll go into a little bit later here, and then, you know,
your [inaudible] guidance is kind of going to guide the structure that we use.
So again, you know, this is going to be the basis of that WBS that we use in reporting
as well, so and again, you know, the remaining documents just kind of outline, you know,
what is actually used to implement the process, and again, you know, we mentioned the reference
up front that we have, the kind of handy-dandy one-slider that kind of outlines some
of these policies, but we just kind of want to quickly hit, you know, why you should comply.
So and, you know, the next slide, right?
-- is slide 13, just kind of walks us through, you know, obviously,
Contracting Officers can kind of use the CSDR data to kind of help,
you know, substantiate contract price.
And, again, some of the language that is outlined here, you know,
specifically kind of empowers, you know, whether it's CADE to, you know,
collect and analyze and maintain the CSDR data.
So again, the CSDR is not, you know, a new process, and it but essentially,
kind of streamlining that data, to capture, you know, some of its ties to CADE, you know,
maybe kind of new to some others.
All right, and then the last kind of point that we want to hit on slide 14, so obviously,
you know, we want to think about how we can help.
I know it's -- I think it may be a little bit of animation on this slide, Jack,
so we can kind of quick just so people can see, but essentially, you know, you know,
that in accordance with some of the FAR guidance, you know,
the Contracting Officer will kind of make determination of, you know,
whether or not that certified, you know, cost and pricing data, and other than certified cost
and pricing data is required, you know, which in turn will, you know, essentially drive,
you know, which analysis, whether it's cost analysis
or pricing analysis will actually be conducted.
So you know, as we kind of discussed in the previous slides, you know, the certified cost
and pricing data, you know, it comes in different flavors but, you know,
CADE can essentially help out value by kind of bridging that gap, to facilitate, you know,
ease of access to the data, you know,
whether that's via a FlexFile, or the legacy 1921 series.
You know, the intent is to kind of help facilitate getting access to that price, profit,
you know, loss and feed data for some of these, you know, contract costs and data reports,
so again, quick overview of, you know, some of the different types of reports and the policy,
you know, that kind of governs them is kind of what we wanted to cover in this initial section.
So what we'll do now is we'll transition to talking about the data that you need in CADE
and I'll turn that over to my colleague to introduce himself.
>> Thank you, Torri.
This is a -- good afternoon, everyone, or I think it's still morning for a few more minutes
in the Central and Pacific Time zones.
My name is Peter Braxton.
I proudly support Torri and our clients, Mr. Tom Henry at the Pentagon as part
of the CADE training team, so Jack, we can go ahead to the next slide.
If you remember nothing else from today, I want you to remember the mantra help us help you.
We have a lot of data that's useful to you, as Torri just said in cost analysis, price analysis
and cost realism analysis so we want to make sure you're aware of all that great data
that we have, that you can make use of.
We do have a help desk in addition to training teams,
so we want to impress upon you the basic data sources you have
if you need help figuring out how to use this site.
We're going to try to do a demo if there's time toward the end today,
but just realize that we're happy to help you with that, at any point.
Where we need your help is getting the CSDRs on contract based on all those policy
and regulations that Torri just went through, so we'll circle back
to that later the training today, but I'm going to focus on what we think the utility
of our data is for the contracting community.
Jack, I think you can click one and we'll bring
up an animation there on the on the earned value.
These basic areas are what we call the pillars of things that we have within CADE.
First and foremost is the cost data there on the left, and so that is the CSDRs and the FlexFile,
so Torri took you through the two pinwheels there,
the FlexFile data, and the legacy data as well.
The second pillar there is earned value data.
That used to be part and parcel of CADE.
It's now in a sister system called the earned value management central repository.
That's probably more useful for the program management folks
that are monitoring the programs as they go.
For us cost analysts and new cost and price analysts out there,
you're probably more interested in the final as-built cost data and that's what you're going
to find in back in that first column.
In the third column you see we have acquisition data.
Now of course there's Dave and to-date there's Damer [phonetic].
They collect a lot of the selected acquisition report data for major programs, the SARs.
We actually have a SAR database in CADE that spans not only 1997 to the present,
which is what you'll find in Damer, but also goes back several decades before that based
on previous Rand and other database work, so that's extremely handy if you're looking
at funding and quantities and cost variances, and other sorts of program level information.
You can find that within our within our site.
The fourth column there is technical, which Torri talked
about that at least three flavors there.
One is the technical data report itself, which can be tailored to the type
of system you're procuring, the software data, the SRDRs,
and also the maintenance and repair data, the M&R.
So those from a costing perspective, those are things that help identify cost drivers,
things we need to scale our actual historical costs by to use in, in our cost analyses be they
for source selection, or independent government cost estimate,
or the sort of milestone cost estimates that we do at CADE and the service cost centers
and the syscoms, and fifth, and finally there,
there's a library column, and that's really a catch all.
There's a number of libraries that provide access to cost research that's used
that can be useful in estimating costs, provide access to acquisition documentation,
so things like ICE memos, independent cost and estimate memos, service cost position,
so you can go back and see the sorts of estimates that have been done
from previous milestones and previous programs, and that should be tremendously helpful
as you're managing your program and doing the contract management for that current program,
so these are just sort of broad categories of data that we have
that we think are eminently useful, and as you can see from the bumper sticker,
the number's always growing, so it's hard for us to keep up with,
but we're talking about thousands of reports, across hundreds of programs going back decades,
so there's a ton of data in here.
We want to help you sort through the haystack and find the needle that's going
to be most useful for your analysis.
If you can go to the next slide.
So this is just a sort of an alternate view.
You saw those five pillars of different cost types.
You see them now sort of arranged on the left hand side.
One thing I'd like to highlight, there's this second item down within
that first arrow called contracts database.
That is a specific database that we're going to find within our data, datasets,
tools and models hub, the DTM hub within the CADE portal, and that has not as wide a range
of programs, as we have for CSDRs, but it's got a lot of good CLIN-level data
and the price changes by CLIN over time, so that's something
that you'll see a graphic from a few slides from now.
We also mentioned in the realm of context, some of the things that you'll find
in the libraries are what we call CAR documents, the cost analysis requirements description.
This is the program and technical baseline that defines an independent cost estimate,
and so often having those details can help you help provide context
to your cost and price analysis.
We've tried to capture those more systematically,
but the historical documentation there can also be very helpful.
And you will find potentially, analysis of alternative, AOA, and IGCE documentation
within the within the CADE library well, so you can see what's been done in past programs,
and that'll help you as you're preparing your analysis for current programs.
On the right hand side there, you see a number of the features that the CADE portal provides.
We are strongly based on user feedback, so we're continually getting feedback primarily
from the cost community, but we'd love that feedback also
from the program management community and the contracting community as well,
so that's why we do these events, to make you aware of the tools that are at your disposal
and to get your feedback, but what we've heard on the cost side
of the world is really, it's all about the data.
